TRANSLATOR'S NOTE

 

In the following text the line numbers in square brackets 
refer to the Greek text (available at Perseus), and the line numbers without brackets 
refer to the English text. Partial lines are normally included with an adjacent 
partial line in the reckoning. The stage directions and endnotes have been 
provided by the translator.

 

In this translation, 
possessives of words ending in -s are usually indicated in the common way (that 
is, by adding 
-âs
 (e.g. 
Zeus
 and 
Zeusâs
). This 
convention adds a syllable to the spoken word (the sound 
-iz
). 
Sometimes, for metrical reasons, this English text indicates such possession in 
an alternate manner, with a simple apostrophe. This form of the possessive does 
not add an extra syllable to the spoken name (e.g., 
Hippolytus 
and 

Hippolytusâ
 are both four-syllable words; whereas, 
Hippolytusâs 
has 
four syllables).
 

The translator would like to acknowledge the extremely 
helpful editorial commentary on the Greek text of 
 

Hippolytus
 by W. S. 
Barrett (Oxford, 1964).

 

 

BACKGROUND NOTE

 

The play 
 
Hippolytus 

 
by the Greek tragedian 
Euripides (c. 480â406 BC) was first performed in Athens in 428 BC as part of the 
trilogy that won first prize in the competition. Of the more than ninety plays 
Euripides is believed to have written, nineteen have survived, as well as some 
fragments of his other plays.

Theseus, king of Athens, and Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, had an 
illegitimate son, Hippolytus. When Hippolyta died, Theseus married Phaedra, 
daughter of Minos, king of Crete. Hippolytus was sent to Troezen, a city in the 
eastern Peloponnese (almost directly across from Athens on the south-western 
side of the Saronic Gulf) to be brought up by Pittheus, grandfather of Theseus. 
Theseus and Phaedra remained in Athens. However, Theseus got into political 
difficulties when he killed some relatives who were challenging him for the 
throne, and he went into temporary and voluntary exile from Athens, moving with 
Phaedra to Troezen. The play begins shortly after Theseus and Phaedra arrive in 
Troezen.

 

 

HIPPOLYTUS

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

 

APHRODITE: goddess of love

HIPPOLYTUS: bastard son of Theseus

SERVANT: an elderly attendant on Hippolytus

NURSE: servant of Phaedra

PHAEDRA: wife of Theseus

THESEUS: exiled king of Athens

MESSENGER: an attendant on Hippolytus

ARTEMIS: virgin goddess of the hunt

CHORUS: young married women of Troezen.

[The play is set in front of the royal palace in Troezen. At the back there 
are large double doors in the centre of the wall of the palace and statues of 
Aphrodite and Artemis on either side, each with an altar in front of it.]

[Enter Aphrodite.]

APHRODITE

I am a powerful goddess, celebrated

in heaven and among all mortal men,

who call me Aphrodite. Of all people

who gaze upon the sunlight and inhabit

regions between the Pillars of Atlas

and the Euxine Sea, I look with favour

on those who give my power due respect,

but I strike
 down all those who, stuffed with pride,

disparage me.
(1)
 
For the family of gods

shares this attributeâthey get great delight                          

10

from those honours human beings bestow.

That this is true I will soon demonstrate.

For Theseus and Hippolyta, an Amazon,                                       

 [10]

had a son, Hippolytus, and this b,

a student trained by pious Pittheus,

is the only person here in Troezen

who claims that I, of all divinities,

by nature am the most despicable.

He refuses to have women in his bed,

turns his back on any thought of marriage,                           

 20

and worships Zeusâs daughter Artemis,

Apolloâs sister, believing her to be

the greatest god of all. He spends his time

in green forests, always in the company

of that virgin goddess, scouring the land

for wild creatures with his swift hunting dogs. 

 

The two enjoy a close relationship,

too close for any mortal with a god.

I bear him no ill will for that. Why should I?                                  
  [20]

But since Hippolytus has slighted me,                                    

30

today I will avenge myself on him.

Most of my scheme is in place alreadyâ

what I have left to do will not be hard.

For Hippolytus went some time ago

from Pittheusâ home to Pandionâs land,

to see and celebrate the secret rites

of sacred Demeter. His fatherâs wife,

the well-born lady Phaedra, saw him there,

and, thanks to what I had 
 

arranged, felt her heart

gripped by fierce desire.
(2)
 
Before moving here,                 
    
 40

to Troezen land, she had a temple built

in Athens, near Pallas Athenaâs rock,

a shrine to Aphrodite. It faced Troezen,                                         
  [30]

to mark her passion for her absent love,

and afterwards she let the people know

she had raised this temple to the goddess

in honour of Hippolytus. But now,

Theseus has left the land of Cecropsâ

he has agreed to live for one whole year

in exile from his people, to
 escape                                          

 50

blood guilt for killing the sons of Pallas.
(3)

He and his wife have now sailed to Troezen,

where she, poor woman, groans in agony,

driven out of her wits by stings of love

and dying in silence. None of her servants                                     
  [40]

knows of her disease. But this passion of hers

must not end like this. I will tell Theseus

about her love, and all will be revealed.

Then that young man who is my enemy

will be killed by his own father, Theseus,                               

60

with one of those wishes he was given,

a gift from Poseidon, lord of the sea,

(the god once said if Theseus prayed to him,

then his prayers would be fulfilled three times).
(4)

As for Phaedra, she is a noble queen,

but nonetheless she dies. Her misfortunes

do not matter all that much, not enough

for me to avenge myself on enemies

in ways that do not satisfy my heart.                                               
[50]

But I see Hippolytus on his way here,                                     

70

returning from all that hard work hunting.

I will leave this place, for he is coming

with a huge throng of servants at his heels,

making a great din, as they howl their hymns

in honour of the goddess Artemis.

He does not realize that Hadesâ gates

are opening for him and this dayâs light

is the last light of day he will ever see.

 

[Enter
 Hippolytus and his 
Attendants, singing and dancing. They move toward the statue and altar of 
Aphrodite on one side of the central doors.]
(5)

 

HIPPOLYTUS

Follow me, come follow me,

and sing of heavenly Artemis,                                                 

 80

great Zeusâs child and our protector!                                              
 [60]

 

HIPPOLYTUS and ATTENDANTS

Hail reverend lady, sacred queen,

hail to the holiest child of Zeus,

daughter born to him from Leto,

and fairest virgin of them all,

inhabiting the spacious heavens

in your illustrious fatherâs home,

the palace of Zeus, made all of gold.

O beautiful one, we welcome you,                                                  

[70]

the loveliest god in all Olympus!                                         
    
 90

 

HIPPOLYTUS 
 

[at the statue of Artemis]

O sovereign goddess, to you I bring

this garland made of woven flowers

gathered in unspoiled meadowlands,

where shepherds dare not graze their flocks

and harvest sickles are still unknown.

In spring, bees fly through pristine fields,

and modest Reverence feeds the land

with purest streams of river dew.

These flowers the virtuous may pick,

the ones who keep a constant rein                                         

 100
   
  [80]

on their desires in all they do,

whose virtue comes from who they are

and not from what they have been taught.

But those who are not pure may not do so.

 

[Hippolytus moves up to the statue of Artemis to 
offer her a flowery wreath.]

 

Dear mistress, accept from my chaste hand

this flowery wreath for your golden hair.

Of mortal men I am the only one

who has the privilege of spending time

alone with you. We converse together,

and though I never gaze upon your face,                               

110

I can hear your voice. I pray my life

will end like this, just as it has begun.

 

SERVANT

My lordâI do not call you âmaster,â

since that title is reserved for gods aloneâ

would you listen if I offered good advice?

 

HIPPOLYTUS

Of course. Otherwise I would look foolish.                                     
[90]

 

SERVANT

You know the rule men are supposed to follow?

 

HIPPOLYTUS

No, I do not. What rule is it you mean?

 

SERVANT

The one that says we ought to hate being proud

and failing to treat everyone politely.                                      

120

 

HIPPOLYTUS

And rightly so. What man swollen with pride

is not annoying?

 

SERVANT

                                      
Is there not some charm

in being courteous?

 

HIPPOLYTUS

                                            
Indeed there isâ

a great deal of charm, and benefits, too,

earned without much effort.

 

SERVANT

                                   
And do you think

the same holds true among the gods?

 

HIPPOLYTUS

                                                           
I doâ

if mortals live by laws from gods above.

 

SERVANT

Why then is there is a famous goddess

you never call by name?

 

HIPPOLYTUS

                                                             Which one is that?

Take careâusing a godâs name may show disrespect!
(7)
       

 130
   
  [100]

 

SERVANT 
 

[pointing to the statue of Aphrodite]

This one here standing right beside your doorsâ

Aphrodite.

 

HIPPOLYTUS

                                               
I practise chastity,

and so I greet that goddess from a distance.

 

SERVANT

But men revere her and celebrate her fame.

 

HIPPOLYTUS

I am not fond of gods worshipped at night.

 

SERVANT

My son, one must pay tribute to the gods.

 

HIPPOLYTUS

But with both gods and men, different people

have different preferences.

 

SERVANT

                                                    
I wish you luck

and all the prudent judgment you may need.

 

HIPPOLYTUS 
 

[turning to his hunting companions]

You attendantsâleave now. Go in the house                        

140

and prepare our meal. After a dayâs hunt

a table full of food is a great treat!                                                  

[110]

And make sure you rub down my horses, too.

When I have eaten my fill, Iâll yoke them

to my chariot and exercise them well.

 

[The Attendants go into the palace. Hippolytus turns 
back to the Servant.]

 

As for that goddess of yours, Aphrodite,

Iâll bid her a fond farewell.

 

[Hippolytus goes into the palace.]

 

SERVANT

                                             
When young men

think as he does, we must not do the same,

and so, great Aphrodite, as I pray

at this statue in your honour, I will use                                
  
150

language that befits a slave. If being young

makes a manâs heart impetuous and proud

and he says foolish things, you should forgive him

and act as if you have not heard. For gods

must show more wisdom than we mortal men.                              
[120]

 

[The Servant goes into the palace. Enter the Chorus 
of Troezen women.]

 

CHORUS

There is a place where water

from the stream of Oceanus

(so people say) seeps from the 
 

rock

and falls from a projecting ledge.
(8)

Here people fill their water jugsâ                                          

160

and here I met a friend of mine

rinsing bright garments in the stream

and spreading them in the warm sun

along the surface of the rock.

There for the first time I heard news

about the queen, my mistress.                                                        
 [130]

She is ill, resting in a sick bed,

staying indoors, with her fair head

wrapped up in finely woven veils.

I hear that for the past three days                                          

 170

her mouth has taken in no food,

for she has kept her body pure,

refusing Demeterâs gifts of grain.

She harbours a secret agony

and wants to dieâto drive her life

to some disastrous final end.                                                           
 [140]

O girl, has some god possessed you?

Is your mind now madly roaming

because of Hecate or Pan,

or the ancient Corybantes,                                                      

 180

or Cybele, our mountain mother?

Are you being punished for some fault

by Dictynna, goddess of wild beasts,

or some impiety? Did you fail

to offer her the sacred cakes?

For she can travel through the sea

and move across dry land that 
 

rises

from eddies in the salty deep.
(9)
                                                      
 [150]

Or is your man the cause of this,

the noble king of the Athenians?                                            

 
190

Is some woman in the palace

having sex with him in secret

in a bed other than your own?

Or in our port that welcomes sailors

has some man from Crete arrived

bearing messages for the queen,

and now she must remain in bed,

her heart weighed down with sorrow

and suffering for family friends?                                                      
 [160]

But womenâs nature tends to show                                         

200

a lack of balanceâin childbirth

a sense of wretched helplessness

combined with utter folly.

Those feelings pierce my womb, as well,

but I call out to Artemis,

guardian goddess of the bow,

who eases all our labour pains.

She never fails to visit meâ

gods be thankedâand is most welcome!
(10)

 

[Enter Nurse and Phaedra with Attendants. the 
servants help Phaedra move to a couch they have brought on.]

 

CHORUS LEADER

But thereâs the old nurse, at the front gate,                           

 210
   
  [170]

bringing Phaedra outside the palace walls.

The cloud of worry in her eyes has grown.

My heart longs to know why the queen is ill,

why her body is so pale and wasted.

 

NURSE

O the troubles we mortals undergo,

the wretched illnesses! What shall I do

to make you comfortable? What do I not do?

Here you are in the fresh air and sunlight.

Your sick bed has been moved outside the house,                        
   [180]

for coming here was all you talked about.                             

  220

But soon enough youâll be hurrying back

to your own rooms again. Youâll be convinced

you were mistaken. Nothing pleases you.

You get no joy from what is here at hand

and find what is not here more pleasurable.

Itâs better to be sick than nurse the sickâ

the first is plain and simple suffering, 

the second mixes sorrow in the heart

with hard work for the hands. But with mortals

all life is pain, and struggles never end.                                 

  230
   
  [190]

Whatever we might yearn for more than life

is surrounded by dark clouds and hidden,

and we seem lovesick for whatever glitters

here on earth, because we have no knowledge

of another way of life. What goes on

beneath the earth is not revealed to us,

and we are vainly swept along by fables.

 

PHAEDRA

Lift up my body and straighten my head.

All my limbs feel weak and sore. You servants,                              
  [200]

help support my hands and these shapely arms.                   

 240

This headdress is too heavy for my head!

Take it from me, and let my hair spread out

across my shoulders.

 

NURSE

                                             
Cheer up, my child!

Stop making such an effort to move around.

This illness will be easier to bear

with composure and a noble frame of mind.

The pain is something mortals must endure.

 

PHAEDRA

Alas! How I wish I could take a drink

of pure fresh water from a dew-fed spring

and lie down, relaxing under poplar trees                              

 250
    
[210]

in the long grass of an uncut meadow.

 

NURSE

My child, what are you going on about?

You should not keep chattering on like this

in front of such a crowdâblurting out words

that make you sound quite mad!

 

PHAEDRA

                                                 
Take me awayâ

up on the mountain! Iâll run in the woods

to the stands of pine where deer-killing hounds

chase down the dappled hind! O by the gods,

how I long to urge on the dogs and hurl                                        
  [220]

a Thessalian spearâto hold in my 
 

hand                                

  260

that pointed shaft next to my golden hair!
(11)

 

NURSE

But why, my child, do you want such things?

Why so desperate to go out hunting?

Why this desire of yours for mountain springs?

There is fresh water here, beside our walls,

a steady stream of it going down the hill.

You can drink there anytime you please.

 

PHAEDRA

O Artemis, queen of Limne near the sea,

the training ground for thundering horses,

I wish I were there, at your racing 
 

school,                              

 270
   
  [230]

breaking in those young Enetian steeds.
(12)

 

NURSE

Why are you babbling words like this again?

You must be disturbed! At one point youâre keen

to set off for the mountains and the huntâ

thatâs what you long for. And then you yearn

for horses on sand untouched by any wave.

This business calls for expert prophecy,

my child, to explain to us which deity

has muddled your wits and driven you mad.

 

PHAEDRA

I am so miserable! What have I done?                                    

280

Why has my mind lost all its common sense?

I was insaneâstruck down with delusions

from some god. Alas, I am so wretched!

O nurse, please cover up my head again.

I am ashamed of what I have just said.

Cover me. My eyes are streaming tears,

and my face betrays my shame. To be sane

is agony, to be mad a dreadful state.

Better to die not knowing anything,

quite ignorant of oneâs own misery.                                       

  290

 

NURSE 
 

[placing a shawl over Phaedraâs face]

Iâll cover you up. But when will death come                                  
   [250]

to cover up my body? A long life

has taught me a great deal: human beings

should pledge affection for one another

not to very marrow of their souls,

but with moderation. Bonds of friendship

linking hearts should be easy to untie,

easy to cast off or tighten. If one heart

bears the pain of two, as I do with her,

thatâs a heavy burden. People do say                                 
    
  300
   
  [260]

too much attention to oneâs way of life

leads to disaster rather than true joy

and is a way of ruining oneâs health.

And so my preference is for self-control

and not excess. Wise men agree with me.

 

CHORUS LEADER

Old nurse, faithful servant of queen Phaedra,

we can see that her condition is not good,

but what her sickness is we do not know.

Weâd like to ask you and hear your answer.                                   
   [270]

 

NURSE

Iâve no idea, though Iâve questioned her.                            
   
  310

She is not willing to say.

 

CHORUS LEADER

                                                            
Not even

how these troubling symptoms first began?

 

NURSE

My answer is the same. She says nothingâ

about all this she will not speak a word.

 

CHORUS LEADER

How weak she is. Her body looks so worn.

 

NURSE

No wonder. She hasnât eaten for three days.

 

CHORUS LEADER

Is she disturbed or trying to kill herself?

 

NURSE

To kill herself? Well, thatâs how it will end,

if she keeps refusing food.

 

CHORUS LEADER

                                     
What you say

is quite astonishing if her husband                                       
 
 320

approves of what sheâs doing.

 

NURSE

                                      
She hides it,

and says she is not sick.

 

CHORUS LEADER

                                       
Canât he guess                                         

    [280]

by looking at her face?

 

NURSE

                                            
How can he?

He happens to be away from Troezen.

 

CHORUS LEADER

Why not try compelling her to tell you

why she is so ill, why her mind wanders?

 

NURSE

Iâve tried all sorts of things without success.

But I wonât give up my efforts even now,

so you people with me here can witness

how I have been acting with my mistress                            
  
  330

in her distress.

 

[The Nurse turns her attention back to Phaedra.]

 

                        
But come now, my dear child,

letâs both forget what we just talked about.

You must be more sociable. Smooth that frown                            
  [290]

and change your attitude. And as for me,

in the past I have not followed what you said

with enough sympathy. Well, Iâll stop that

and find a different and a better way.

If you are sick with one of those illnesses

we do not talk about, these women here

can help you cope with that condition.                                
  
 340

But if whatâs wrong may be discussed with men,

then speak up, so we can talk about it

with physicians.

 

[The Nurse waits for a reply, but Phaedra says 
nothing.]

 

                               
Why are you still silent?

You should not remain so quiet, my child.

But if Iâve said something wrong, correct me,

or else accept the good advice I offer.

Say something! Look at me!

 

[Phaedra remains silent.]

 

                                                 
I feel wretched!                              

  [300]

Ladies, the work weâre doing here is useless.

Weâre no better off than we were before.

Our words did not calm her down earlier,                          
   
 350

and now she is not listening to us.

 

[The Nurse turns back to Phaedra.]

 

In this matter you can be more stubborn

than the sea, but you should understand thisâ

if you die, you will have betrayed your sons,

who will have no share in their fatherâs goods.
(13)

I swear by that horse-riding Amazon queen

who gave birth to a man whoâll rule your sonsâ

born a bastard, but with royal ambitions.

You know him wellâHippolytus.                                                   
  [310]

 

PHAEDRA

                                                        
O no!

 

NURSE

Does that upset you?

 

PHAEDRA

                 
Nurse, you are destroying me!                          
     
 360

By the gods I beg you to say nothing

about that manâdonât mention him again!

 

NURSE

You see? Your mind is fine, but even so,

though your thoughts are clear, you are not willing

to help out your own sons and save your life.

 

PHAEDRA

I love my children. A different problem

is causing me distress.

 

NURSE

                                      
My child, your hands are,

I assume, not stained with someoneâs blood?

 

PHAEDRA

My hands are pure, but my heart has been polluted.

 

NURSE 

Surely someone who is your enemy                                   
     
 370

has not cast a spell on you?

 

PHAEDRA

                                                       
No. A friend

has been my downfall, though neither of us

wants that to happen.

 

NURSE

                                          
What about Theseus?

Has he committed some wrong against you?                                
    [320]

 

PHAEDRA

May no one find that I have ever harmed him!

 

NURSE

What is this terrible thing that makes you

want to die?

 

PHAEDRA

                        
Let me make my own mistakesâ

I am not harming you.

 

NURSE

                                     
No, not willingly, 
 

but if you perish, it will be my fault.

 

[The Nurse kneels beside Phaedraâs couch and grasps 
her hands.]

 

PHAEDRA

What are you doing? You are too violent,                         
     
 380

clutching my hand like that!

 

NURSE

                                       
And your knees,
 too!

I will not let go!
(14)

 

PHAEDRA

                                        
You wretched woman,

if you learn the truth, you will face disaster!

 

NURSE

What could be worse for me than losing you?

 

PHAEDRA

You will be destroyed. However, for me

this affair brings honour.

 

NURSE

                                             
If it is noble,                                        
  [330]

why refuse to tell me when I ask you?

 

PHAEDRA

I am striving to turn a great disgrace

into something fine.

 

NURSE

                                          
If you reveal it,

will not your honour be even greater?                                
    
 390

 

PHAEDRA

For the sake of the gods, release my hands

and leave.

 

NURSE

                   
Noâyou have not yet given me

the gift I am entitled to receive.

 

PHAEDRA

I willâfor I respect your suppliant hand.

 

[The Nurse releases Phaedraâs hands and stands up.]

 

NURSE

Then Iâll remain silent. From this point on

itâs up to you to speak.

 

PHAEDRA

                                      
O my poor mother,

what passion you felt!

 

NURSE

                              
The way she loved that bull?

Is that what you are talking about, my child?

 

PHAEDRA

And you, too, my 
 

unfortunate sister,

bride of Dionysus!
(15)

 

NURSE

                      
Whatâs wrong with you?                              
     
  400
  
   [340]

Why abuse your family in this way?

 

PHAEDRA

I am the thirdâand now I am dying

in such misery!

 

NURSE

                                                           
This amazes me!

The things youâre saying! What are you getting at?

 

PHAEDRA

Whatâs happening is an old misfortuneâ

this trouble is not new.

 

NURSE

                                    
That tells me nothing.

I have still not heard what I need to know.

 

PHAEDRA

Alas! How I wish you could be the one

to say the things I have to tell you!

 

NURSE

Iâm no prophet able to see clearly                                      
     
 410

what lies hidden from sight.

 

PHAEDRA

                                           
What do people mean

when they use the expression âbeing in loveâ?

 

NURSE

Something very pleasurable, my child,

but at the same time painful.

 

PHAEDRA

                                                   
I would say

what I have is that second feelingâpain.

 

NURSE

What are you talking about, my child?                                           
  [350]

You mean you are in love? Who is the man?

 

PHAEDRA

Iâm not sure what he calls himself . . . the son

of that Amazon . . .

 

NURSE
